title: Length-preserving shard corruption
scope_and_topology: Single process, CPU. Synthetic dataset of 3 shards x 40 timesteps x 8 sensors, each shard's SHA-256 and byte length recorded in shards.json at creation time.
hypothesis: A shard modified after preprocessing (partial write, bad disk, interrupted sync, stale object-store retry) will not announce itself; training proceeds and produces a loss curve.
detection_signal: Declared before injection: ShardManifest.verify() runs before the first optimizer step and rejects the dataset, naming the offending file and reporting sha256 mismatch. A size check alone was declared insufficient in advance, so the injected corruption is length-preserving.
injection: corrupt_file_bytes() XORs 16 bytes at offset 100 of shard 1 in place; the test asserts file length is unchanged so only the digest can catch it.
diagnosis: Three failure modes are kept distinct rather than collapsed into one bad-data error: size mismatch indicates truncation or partial write; sha256 mismatch with correct size indicates in-place modification or bit rot; a missing shard indicates incomplete sync or a wrong dataset root.
intervention: Verification runs before the first optimizer step, so the run aborts having spent no compute. The remedy is to re-fetch the shard and re-verify against the same manifest; the manifest is never regenerated to clear the error, which would record the corruption as canonical.

verification.detail: Corruption, truncation and absence are each detected and named; restoring the bytes re-verifies clean.

counterfactual: Without the digest gate the corrupted region would decode to arbitrary float values including NaN, surfacing as a loss spike or silent NaN propagation and being misattributed to the learning rate or to instability - a plausible but wrong diagnosis costing hours and possibly a restart.
limitations: Detects corruption at rest before a run; does not detect corruption occurring mid-run after verification. Synthetic fixtures only. SHA-256 over whole files identifies the offending file, not the offending byte range. Single process; verifying identical bytes across hosts is a Phase C concern.
